FOR INDEPENDENT INTERIOR PAINTERS

Bid the surfaces, not the floor plan.

Price an interior painting job the way the trade actually estimates one: each surface divided by the production rate you really hit, extra coats at a fraction of first-coat time, then paint, payroll burden, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep. You get the job price, what it works out to per floor square foot, and the number below which the job loses money.

The house

One row per surface. Production rate is how much of that surface one painter covers per hour on the first coat — pick a type to start from a common figure, then replace it with a rate timed from your own jobs.

SurfaceQuantityRateCoats

Your costs

Extra-coat factor is second-coat time as a fraction of first-coat hours — not a second full first coat. Ceiling height only slows wall rows; trim and doors stay on their own rates. The common $/sq ft field is the rule of thumb homeowners quote; it is scored against your cost, not recommended as a price.

Where the labor goes

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting production rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a benchmark, or a guarantee — time your own jobs and replace them.

    Common questions

    How much should I charge per square foot to paint a room?

    Per floor square foot is the number that loses painters money, because trim and doors take a large share of the day and almost none of the floor area. This tool works the other way round: each surface is divided by its own production rate — walls in sq ft per hour, trim in linear feet per hour, doors and windows and cabinet pieces per hour — and the price comes out of those hours. If you enter the floor area anyway, it shows you the resulting $/floor sq ft, and it will score a rule-of-thumb $/sq ft figure against your actual cost so you can see whether the competitive-looking number is below break-even.

    Why isn't a second coat double the labor?

    Because it usually isn't. Extra coats are priced at a fraction of first-coat hours — 0.65 by default, which you can change — since there is less cutting and wet-on-dry rolls faster. Paint quantity, on the other hand, does scale with coats: gallons are paintable area × coats × (1 + waste) ÷ the coverage per gallon. So a second coat adds about 65% of the labor and 100% of the paint.

    How does ceiling height change the price?

    Through a ladder-and-staging factor on wall hours only: 1.0 up to 9 ft, 1.12 to 10 ft, 1.3 to 12 ft, and 1.55 above that. The square footage of a tall wall is already in the quantity you entered; the factor is for the time lost setting up to reach it. It does not apply to ceilings, trim, doors, windows, or cabinets, because those are not slowed by wall height in the same way. The steps are a coarse starting adjustment, not a scaffolding quote.

    Where do prep and setup hours go?

    They are separate lines, added to the surface hours before anything is priced — patching, sanding, caulking, and masking in prep, and daily setup, protection, and cleanup in setup. Keeping them out of the production rates is the point: a rate timed on clean walls stays reusable across jobs, and the repaint of a hundred-year-old house is priced by its prep hours rather than by quietly inventing a slower rate you then forget to undo next time.

    Why isn't a 25% margin the same as adding 25% to my cost?

    Margin here is a share of the final price — price = job cost ÷ (1 − margin) — because that is how the customer's number reads and how your books read it. Overhead is different: it is a markup on the direct cost of the job, applied before margin and never to itself or to the profit. Marking a $4,000 cost up 25% gives $5,000, which is a 20% margin. Targeting a 25% margin gives $5,333. On a full-season book that difference is several weeks of pay.

    Is my pricing data uploaded anywhere?

    No. No account, no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser, and the shareable link carries your inputs in the URL rather than through a server. The business details saved for the printed proposal live in this browser's local storage and "Forget my business details" clears them. The optional local usage counter records only which features were used and the day, never your rates, wages, or prices.

    Hand the customer a proposal

    The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

    Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

    No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, financial, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. Verify every figure against your own payroll, insurance, and material costs, and against a qualified professional, before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

    Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device. A shareable link carries only the numbers you typed, inside the URL you copy. Usage counts are anonymous tallies of which features were used, stored locally, and never include your house, wages, costs, or prices.

    Pricing an exterior elevation instead of interior rooms? The exterior painting bid calculator prices stories, scrape and prime, and hard access — nothing uploaded.

← Painting bid calculator

Why a $2 per square foot interior painting bid loses money

Homeowners and discount competitors quote interior painting as a price per floor square foot. That number is easy to say and usually wrong. Floor area is not paintable area, and the surfaces that take the day — trim, doors, second coats, prep — barely show up on the floor plan.

The free painting bid calculator prices the job from production rates instead. Below is the same arithmetic on a typical 1,200 sq ft, 8-foot-ceiling, 3-bedroom interior, using the calculator's starting inputs so you can open the tool and change them.

Open the bid calculator

What a $2/sq ft bid actually is

On 1,200 floor square feet, $2/sq ft is a $2,400 job. That sounds like a day's work plus paint. It is not. The same house has roughly 2,400 sq ft of walls, 1,200 sq ft of ceilings, 320 linear feet of trim, eight doors, and ten windows. Those are the hours.

Where the hours go

Using starting production rates — 200 sq ft of wall per hour on the first coat, 175 on ceilings, 50 linear feet of trim, 1.25 doors, 2.5 windows — and a 0.65 extra-coat factor:

  • Walls, two coats: about 20 hours
  • Ceilings, two coats: about 11 hours
  • Trim, two coats: about 11 hours
  • Doors, two coats: about 11 hours
  • Windows, one coat: 4 hours
  • Prep and setup: 8 hours

That is about 64 labor hours. Trim and doors together rival the wall time, and they contribute almost nothing to the floor-square-foot figure the homeowner is arguing from.

Then add paint and burden

At a $25 wage and 25% payroll burden, those hours are already about $2,000 in loaded labor before paint. Paint at 350 sq ft per gallon, two coats, 10% waste, and $45/gallon is another several hundred dollars. Overhead and a 25% target margin sit on top of that. The walk-away price — total job cost, before any profit — is above $2,400 on these inputs. A $2/sq ft bid is then a losing bid, not a competitive one.

What to do instead

Estimate surfaces, not floor plans. Time a few of your own jobs and replace the starting rates. Enter a price already on the table and see whether it clears your walk-away number. The calculator does that arithmetic in the browser and does not upload the job.

Price your next interior with the calculator

Common questions

Why do interior painters lose money bidding per square foot?

Price per floor square foot cannot see trim, doors, coats, prep, or ceiling height. Those surfaces take labor hours that never appear in the floor plan, so a $2/sq ft bid on a typical 3-bedroom house can sit below the job's own cost.

How should an interior painting job be estimated?

Estimate each surface from a production rate (how much of that surface one painter covers per hour), add extra coats at a fraction of first-coat time, then add prep, paint, payroll burden, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep.

No warranty. This page is not legal, tax, financial, or business advice, and it does not tell anyone what to charge. The figures are arithmetic on the calculator's published starting inputs. Verify every number against your own payroll and material costs before relying on it or submitting a bid.

vs-a-flat-2-per-square-foot-bid.html.text:
← Painting Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat $2 a square foot bid

“$2 a square foot” is not a price for an interior repaint — it is a price for one specific room's worth of trim, doors, and windows, quietly applied to every house that calls in.

What a flat price per square foot is

A flat rate per square foot is the fastest way to quote a repaint: multiply the floor area by a number and read off a price. It is the number a homeowner holding a discount competitor's postcard or a search-result special will call and ask you to match, whatever their house actually needs.

The number behind it was set for one job — bare walls and ceilings, no trim, no doors, no windows, one coat — and then reused for every repaint afterward, whether or not the next house looks anything like the room the rate was built on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each surface — walls, ceilings, trim, doors, windows, cabinets — with its own quantity, production rate, and coat count, plus your own labor wage, paint cost, and target margin. It prices the trim, the doors, and the windows separately by kind, then returns the walk-away price and a bid price above your target margin — for this house, not a generic one.

What a flat price per square foot doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same $/sq ft whether a house has zero linear feet of trim or 320, even though every foot of trim adds its own hours and its own paintable area the floor plan never counts. Prices trim separately as its own hours and its own paintable area, so a trim-heavy house costs more than a flat floor of the same size.
Has no line for doors, windows, or cabinet doors, regardless of whether the house has none or a dozen of each. Prices doors, windows, and cabinets separately by count and production rate, so a house with more of them costs more than one without.
Charges the same rate for one coat as for two, even though a second coat runs a real fraction of first-coat time on every surface. Prices extra coats per surface at a disclosed factor of first-coat time, so a two-coat job costs more than a one-coat job of the same area.
Gives the estimator a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the walk-away price and the dollar gap against a flat per-square-foot rate, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two houses, the same floor-blind rate

Using this calculator's own shipped starting rates ($25/hr wage, 25% burden, $45/gallon paint at 350 sq ft coverage, 10% waste, 15% overhead, a 25% target margin):

JobThis calculator's priceThe flat $2.19/sq ft rateGap
400 sq ft room, bare walls and ceilings, two coats, no trim, no doors, no windows — the job the rate is set from$875.56 bid price; $656.67 break-even cost$875.56 (exactly $2.19/sq ft — this rate is fit to this job)No gap on the job the rate was built on.
1,200 sq ft house, two-coat walls and ceilings, 320 lf of trim, 8 doors, 10 windows — a typical 3-bedroom$4,988.47 bid price; $3,741.35 break-even cost$2,626.68The rate quotes $1,114.67 below this job's own break-even cost — before a dollar of profit — and $2,361.79 below the calculator's own bid price.

The $2.19/sq ft rate is not invented — it is this calculator's own price on the bare-room job, divided by that job's own floor square footage. It fits that one job by construction. Applied to the trim-and-door-heavy 3-bedroom, it prices only the 1,200 sq ft of floor and never sees the trim, doors, or windows at all. Run your own house's numbers in the calculator to see where it falls.

A flat per-square-foot rate is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one room it was built for, and nothing about a flat number tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not know your local market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat price per square foot get an interior painting bid wrong?

Because the cost driver is trim, doors, windows, cabinets, coat count, and ceiling height — not the floor square footage a homeowner measures. A 1,200 sq ft house with 320 linear feet of trim and eight doors is doing far more work than a 1,200 sq ft house of bare walls and ceilings, none of which shows up in the floor plan.

What does a flat price per square foot usually leave out entirely?

Trim, doors, windows, and cabinet doors — surfaces that take real labor hours and paint but contribute almost nothing to the floor-square-foot figure a homeowner argues from. A second coat and above-standard ceiling height are also invisible to a flat rate.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped starting rates: a 400 sq ft room of bare walls and ceilings prices at $875.56, or $2.19 a floor square foot. Applying that same $2.19 rate to a 1,200 sq ft house with 320 linear feet of trim, eight doors, and ten windows quotes $2,626.68, which is $1,114.67 below that job's own $3,741.35 break-even cost, before a dollar of profit, and $2,361.79 below the calculator's own $4,988.47 bid price.

Is a flat price per square foot ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of near-identical jobs — same trim length, same door and window count, same coat count — a per-square-foot rate can land close, and on this calculator's own bare-room preset it is exactly the rate that job supports, because it was set from that job. The risk is applying the same rate outside that band without noticing, because the rate does not know how much trim the next house has and neither does the estimator until the surfaces are actually counted.

Does this calculator know what paint or labor cost in my market?

No. It has no data on local material or labor rates. It takes each surface's quantity and production rate, coats, prep and setup hours, paint price and coverage, wage, and burden, and turns that into a price for this job — the arithmetic a flat per-square-foot rate skips, not a market survey.

Open the Painting Bid Calculator to price your own job, or read why a $2 per square foot interior painting bid loses money.

No warranty. This free tool is not painting, construction, legal, tax, or financial advice, and it does not replace a qualified professional. Verify every figure against your own payroll and material costs before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number on this page and in the calculator stays on this device; this page names no company, product, or service, so it makes no claim about how anyone else prices a job.

vs-paintscout.html.text:
← Painting Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. PaintScout

Two different shapes: PaintScout is an account-based platform for running a painting company's whole sales pipeline. This page is a free, private, no-account worksheet for one number — whether the price for one interior repaint, estimated by production rate per surface, actually clears your cost and margin.

What each tool is for

PaintScout is a cloud-based sales and estimating platform built specifically for painting contractors — it is not a generic construction or field-service tool. It is built around producing an on-site estimate in minutes from built-in production rates, turning that estimate into a proposal a customer can review and approve, and running the leads, quotes, change orders, and invoicing tied to those jobs through one account, used across every job a painting company sells, on an ongoing subscription. PaintScout's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific feature list, plan names, or pricing, so only its well-documented identity and category are stated here: nothing about it is invented, and no dollar figure for it appears on this page.

This calculator does none of that. It does not track a lead, send a proposal for a customer to approve online, or hold a record across jobs. It takes one interior repaint — each surface's quantity and your own timed production rate, an extra-coat factor, prep and setup hours, paint quantity from coverage and waste, payroll burden, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep — and turns that into the job price, the price per floor square foot, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away number below which the job loses money, plus a printable customer proposal with a scope, deposit split, and price-held date. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

QuestionWhere to answer it
I need to track leads, send customer-facing proposals for online approval, and run job costing across every repaint my company sells.PaintScout, or a comparable painting business platform — running the whole pipeline is not something this calculator does.
Does the price for this one interior job actually clear my cost and target margin, once trim, doors, coats, prep, and overhead are counted correctly?This calculator — free, instant, private, no account.
Why does a low, round per-floor-square-foot bid on this house lose money once trim and doors are counted?This calculator's own per-square-foot walkthrough.
I need my whole sales team estimating and quoting from one shared account.PaintScout — built as an ongoing, account-based platform for exactly that job.
Do I need to create an account or sign up to use the tool?This calculator: no. PaintScout's tools are used through a paid account.

Most painting contractors get different value from each: PaintScout (or a comparable platform) for running the company's whole sales-to-proposal pipeline as an ongoing account, and a private calculator like this one for an instant, no-login check on whether one interior repaint's price actually clears cost and margin before the bid goes out. This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a project record, a customer proposal sent through an account, or a coverage or substrate determination.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Common questions

Should I use this calculator or PaintScout?

They do different jobs. PaintScout is a painting-only sales and estimating platform used by painting contractors to build on-site estimates, send proposals a customer can approve, and run leads and jobs through one account as a business, on an ongoing subscription. This calculator does none of that. It takes one interior repaint's surfaces — walls, ceilings, trim, doors, windows — each divided by its own production rate, adds prep, setup, paint, payroll burden, overhead, and the margin you intend to keep, and turns that into the job price, the price per floor square foot, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price below which the job loses money, plus a printable customer proposal, instantly, in the browser, with no account and nothing uploaded. A painting company running leads, a sales team, and job records across every project it sells is better served by PaintScout or a comparable platform; a painter who wants an instant, private, correctly-estimated price for one job before a bid goes out is in the right place here.

Is this page affiliated with PaintScout?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by PaintScout. PaintScout is a trademark of its owner, named here only to describe what this calculator is and is not.
